moduleTitle: The meaning and purpose of life

note.specFocus: Christian and non-religious views on what gives life meaning and purpose.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
2.2 The Meaning and Purpose of Life
Christians and non-religious people often answer the question "what is life for?" very differently.
Christian teaching
• The Westminster Shorter Catechism summarises Christian purpose succinctly: "man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever."
• Jesus taught that the greatest commandments are to love God fully and to love one's neighbour as oneself (Mark 12:30–31); for Christians, purpose is found in relationship with God and in service to others.
• Building the "Kingdom of God" — working for justice, peace and love in the world — is seen by many Christians as part of their life's purpose, following Jesus' example and teaching.
Non-religious views
• Humanists find meaning through relationships, creativity, learning, contributing to society and helping others flourish, without appeal to God or an afterlife.
• Because this life is believed to be the only one, Humanists argue it should be treated as uniquely precious, giving strong motivation to live well and ethically now.
Comparing the views
• Both views can lead to similar ethical behaviour (kindness, honesty, service) but differ on the ultimate source and permanence of meaning — eternal relationship with God versus value created within a single finite life.
Exam link: "Evaluate" questions on this topic reward showing you understand both sources of meaning can motivate genuinely good lives, rather than assuming only religious people can live meaningfully.

questions.examTip: Make two separate points and develop each one. Link the development directly to the question.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. Many Christians would summarise life's purpose using the Westminster Shorter Catechism's statement that "man's chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him forever", meaning a relationship with God is the central purpose of human life.

2. Jesus taught that the greatest commandments are to love God with all one's heart, soul, mind and strength, and to love one's neighbour as oneself (Mark 12:30–31), so for Christians, life's purpose also involves showing love and service to other people.
questions.question: Choose one religion. Outline two teachings about the meaning and purpose of life.

questions.examTip: For a 12-mark evaluation, use accurate religious teaching, explain different religious or non-religious views, analyse the statement and reach a justified conclusion. The conclusion should follow from the arguments you have discussed.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: Many Christians would argue that without God, there is no ultimate, objective source of meaning or value; purpose would simply be invented by individuals and would not outlast death, making it seem arbitrary.

A second consideration is: Christians often root purpose in loving and serving God and in the hope of eternal life, so that even hardship in this life has lasting significance as part of a larger relationship with God.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Humanists strongly reject this, arguing that purpose can come from relationships, creativity, learning, helping others and contributing to human flourishing; the Humanist view is that this one life is precious precisely because it is the only one we have, which gives strong motivation to live it well.

A further consideration is: Many non-religious people live deeply meaningful, ethical lives focused on family, work and community, showing that a sense of purpose does not appear to depend on religious belief in practice.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: whether "purpose" requires an eternal or divine foundation to count as genuine, or whether purpose can be built entirely from human relationships and achievements within this one life. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.

questions.question: Explain two Christian views about meaning and purpose of life. Include a source, tradition or example where relevant.

questions.examTip: Use accurate Christian teaching, explain why each point matters, and in an evaluation compare arguments before reaching a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of love of God and neighbour, vocation, discipleship, stewardship and service and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
